title: How To Stay The Course With A Tough Class
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin addresses the mental toughness required to remain consistent with a difficult class, opening with a Winston Churchill quote about being 'a peg, hammered into the frozen ground, immovable.' He offers three mindset shifts for staying the course: committing to consequences 'for them,' as a protective duty toward students; adopting a willingness to lose one's job rather than abandon promises, which paradoxically secures greater respect and job security; and accepting that consistent accountability is the only path to revealing the best in students who currently seem disrespectful or unmotivated. Linsin frames misbehavior in a tough class as the product of past inconsistency and poor leadership rather than students' true nature. He closes with a personal anecdote about imagining even the President having to follow classroom rules, underscoring that cultivating this tough mindset is valuable for any teacher, not just those facing extreme challenges.
points: Staying consistent with a tough class requires deliberate mental toughness, since resistance to following through is universal and never comes naturally.
Framing consequences as protecting students' right to learn ('do it for them') makes follow-through feel like duty rather than confrontation.
Adopting an uncompromising 'they'll have to drag me out' mindset paradoxically leads to greater job security and colleague and student respect, not less.
Disrespectful, unmotivated behavior in a difficult class is typically the result of past inconsistency and poor leadership, not the students' true character.
Fair, honest, and consistent accountability is presented as the only route to revealing the best in both students and the teacher.
quotes: The tougher the class, the easier it is to be inconsistent. The easier it is to give in and lose control.
You must be, as Winston Churchill once said, “a peg, hammered into the frozen ground, immovable.
There is no one else to safeguard your students from disruption, bullying, being made fun of, and the like but you.
Ironically, with this mindset, not only will you never lose your job, but you’ll be admired by your colleagues, beloved by your students, and left alone by your principal.
When your class is out of control and the students seem so disrespectful, callous, and unmotivated, what you're seeing isn't who they really are.
In fact, in time it will become not just an attitude or mentality you carry with you to school every day. But who you are.
